lesson.title: Zooming Out: How Species Share a Neighborhood
lesson.summary: Community ecology studies how populations of different species living in the same area interact with and influence one another, extending the single-species focus of population ecology to the level of an entire interacting assemblage of species.
lesson.body:
Everything covered so far, exponential and logistic growth, carrying capacity, density dependence, survivorship, life history strategy, has focused on a single population at a time: how one species' numbers change over time in response to its environment. But no population exists in isolation. A forest is not just a population of oak trees; it also contains populations of insects that feed on those oaks, birds that nest in them, fungi that decompose fallen leaves, and countless other species, all sharing the same physical space and affecting each other's fortunes. An ecological community is precisely this: all the populations of different species living and interacting within a given area at a given time.

This sits at a specific point in the broader hierarchy of ecological organization. A single organism belongs to a population, a population is one species' individuals in an area; multiple populations of different species together make up a community; a community together with the nonliving, abiotic environment it interacts with, exchanging energy and cycling nutrients, makes up an ecosystem; ecosystems in turn scale up to biomes and ultimately the biosphere. Community ecology occupies the level between population ecology and ecosystem ecology: it asks not just how large one species' population is, but how the presence, absence, or abundance of other species changes that.

This shift in scale changes the kinds of questions that become answerable. Population ecology alone can describe a rabbit population's growth rate and carrying capacity in isolation, but it cannot explain why that carrying capacity might drop sharply if a new competitor species moves in, or rise if a major predator disappears. Community ecology is what supplies that missing piece, by explicitly studying how interacting populations shape one another's population dynamics rather than treating each species' numbers as determined purely by its own birth and death rates.

Ecologists describe communities using several structural properties: species richness, simply the number of different species present, species diversity, which additionally accounts for how evenly abundance is distributed among those species rather than one or two species dominating, and the presence of particularly influential species whose effects on the rest of the community are disproportionate to their own abundance. A temperate forest community, a coral reef community, and a tallgrass prairie community each have their own characteristic richness, diversity, and set of dominant or influential species, shaped by the specific interactions happening among their member populations.

Those interactions come in several recognizable types, competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism, mutualism, and commensalism among them, each with a different pattern of costs and benefits to the species involved. The next chapter introduces this full set of interspecific interactions, before later chapters look more closely at predation and herbivory specifically.
